defaults.permitted_development: Across Shropshire, a new or altered boundary treatment can rely on permitted development up to 1 metre by the highway and 2 metres in other positions. The important exceptions are heritage curtilages, Article 4 areas and schemes that increase an already excessive height. That fallback can disappear where an Article 4 direction or an old planning condition has removed the normal householder right.

rules.height_rules: Across Shropshire, for ordinary houses, most fence and wall questions come back to the same split between the 1 metre highway-side limit and the 2 metre limit elsewhere.
rules.depth_rules: Across Shropshire, means of enclosure are not controlled by an extension-style depth formula. Height, siting and visual effect do the main planning work.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Shropshire, the same boundary treatment can be acceptable in one position and need permission in another once it fronts a road or sits on a prominent corner.
rules.roof_rules: Across Shropshire, a simple gate or wall is one thing; a roofed gate feature can be quite another. Covered entrance elements should not be assumed to sit within the same fallback.
rules.materials_rules: Across Shropshire, national planning rules focus on height and siting rather than a fixed material list, but visible front boundaries should still use finishes that suit the house and street. Heritage areas are more demanding on detail.

The important exceptions are heritage curtilages, Article 4 areas and schemes that increase an already excessive height. restrictions.conservation_area: In conservation areas, even modest boundary changes can need fuller scrutiny where an existing wall, railing or gate helps define the street scene.
restrictions.listed_building: If the property is listed, or the boundary adjoins listed curtilage structures, changing the enclosure can need listed building consent as well as planning review.
restrictions.article4_notes: Normal enclosure rights can be withdrawn by Article 4 directions or by conditions on the property, which is why front-boundary work sometimes still needs an application.

rules.permitted_development: Boundary walls, fences and gates are usually permitted development if they stay no higher than 1 metre next to a highway used by vehicles and no higher than 2 metres elsewhere, or if an already-higher boundary is altered without increasing its height. That fallback can disappear where an Article 4 direction or an old planning condition has removed the normal householder right.

rules.height_rules: For ordinary houses, most fence and wall questions come back to the same split between the 1 metre highway-side limit and the 2 metre limit elsewhere.
rules.depth_rules: Means of enclosure are not controlled by an extension-style depth formula. Height, siting and visual effect do the main planning work.
rules.boundary_rules: Front and corner boundaries usually face the tightest control. Rear boundaries are generally less constrained than road-facing ones.
rules.roof_rules: Canopies or roofed gate features need their own planning check.
rules.materials_rules: Material choice is usually a design issue rather than a standalone permitted-development test, although listed-building and conservation-area contexts can make inappropriate boundary finishes much harder to defend.

restrictions.conservation_area: A fence or wall in a conservation area may need more than a simple height check, especially if demolition of an older boundary is part of the scheme.
restrictions.listed_building: If the property is listed, or the boundary adjoins listed curtilage structures, changing the enclosure can need listed building consent as well as planning review.
restrictions.article4_notes: Do not rely on the normal 1 metre or 2 metre rule where Article 4 controls or earlier planning conditions remove those householder rights.
